title: Methodology
text: The model is a New Keynesian DSGE solved in Julia, validated to machine precision against an original Dynare 6.3 implementation. The full methodology brief is in the project repository as a 30-page LaTeX PDF. This page is a high-level summary; serious readers should go to the brief.

title: Methodology
text:
Model
A standard New Keynesian three-equation core, augmented with Smets-Wouters frictions:

IS curve with consumption habit (\(h\)): real spending depends on a habit-adjusted Euler equation.
Phillips curve with price indexation (\(\chi_p\)): half of price-setters mechanically index to lagged inflation.
Taylor rule with interest rate smoothing (\(\rho_i\)): the Fed adjusts gradually toward its target rate.

The attack is modeled as a standardized exogenous shock to the Fed’s perceived output gap. The Fed’s perception filter is Kalman-style:
\[\widetilde{ygap}_t = (1 - K) \cdot \rho_p \cdot \widetilde{ygap}_{t-1} + K \cdot (ygap_t + \nu_t + \text{attack}_t)\]
where \(K \in [0, 1]\) is the filter weight on the raw nowcast signal. \(K = 1\) is a naive Fed that trusts the signal; \(K = 0\) is a fully defended Fed that ignores it.

title: Methodology
text:
Calibration grid
The 220-point grid sweeps:

\(\kappa\) (Phillips slope) over \(\{0.06, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20\}\)
\(h\) (habit) over \(\{0.0, 0.4, 0.7\}\)
\(K\) (filter weight) over \(\{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}\)

Each point is a full DSGE solution (impulse-response functions over 16 quarters, 80-quarter welfare loss, three shocks).

title: Methodology
text:
Welfare metric
Standard NK loss function: \(L = \text{var}(\pi) + 0.5 \cdot \text{var}(ygap)\), computed as the sum of squared IRF contributions across the three shocks (productivity, monetary policy, attack).

title: Methodology
text:
Validation
The Julia implementation (MacroModelling.jl) was validated to machine precision against an original Dynare 6.3 implementation of the same equations. IRF differences across the two solvers are below \(10^{-10}\) at all horizons.

title: Methodology
text:
Code and data
All code is in the project repository. The pre-computed cache used by this story is in results/dash_cache_*.csv; the Julia pre-compute script is scripts/precompute_dash_cache.jl.
The full methodology brief is at methodology_brief.pdf. The non-economist companion primer is at companion_primer.pdf.

title: If you can fool the Fed’s nowcast, you can move tens of billions of dollars.
text:
A working paper on AI and monetary policy




Every major central bank now reads the economy in real time through machine-learning models that ingest scraped public-web data. We modeled what happens when an adversary contaminates the inputs.


By John Blakeslee · Updated April 2026
Welfare loss with and without attack, across three Fed filter regimes. The defended regime (K = 0) eliminates the attack-induced loss entirely. The cost is that the Fed becomes less responsive to genuine real shocks, raising baseline loss modestly.

title: If you can fool the Fed’s nowcast, you can move tens of billions of dollars.
section: A new kind of attack surface
text:
A new kind of attack surface
Through the 2010s and 2020s, central banks pushed past the slow drip of official statistics. The Bank for International Settlements has tracked the shift in its annual reports for years. Every major central bank now runs some version of a real-time nowcast pipeline. The pipelines synthesize scraped price data, credit-card transaction aggregates, job-posting feeds, satellite imagery of major ports, and social-media sentiment. They produce daily-frequency estimates of output and inflation, well before the Bureau of Labor Statistics or the Bureau of Economic Analysis publish anything official.
These pipelines have a property that traditional government statistics do not. The Bureau of Labor Statistics gathers payroll data through air-gapped survey infrastructure, encrypted transfers, and rigorous internal validation. It is exceedingly difficult to tamper with payroll employment data without detection. A nowcast pipeline ingests the open web. By design.
In 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department warned that “data poisoning, data leakage, and data integrity attacks can take place at any stage of the AI development and supply chain.” The same year, a Russian information operation called Pravda showed the world the warning was concrete. The American Sunlight Project documented 3.6 million auto-generated articles published across the network in 2024 alone. The articles were not designed to be read by humans; many of the sites lacked basic functionality. They were designed to be ingested by the large-language models and search summarizers that have begun to source the open web.
Newsguard ran an independent audit. Across 450 separate prompts to ten of the most popular AI chatbots, those models referenced 92 distinct Pravda articles. One in three returned Kremlin narratives directly. The Russian propagandist John Mark Dougan, on Russian state media, did not bother to obscure the strategy: “By pushing these Russian narratives from the Russian perspective, we can actually change worldwide AI.”
A central bank’s nowcast pipeline is the same kind of system as a chatbot’s retrieval layer. Less famous, consequential in a way a chatbot is not.

title: If you can fool the Fed’s nowcast, you can move tens of billions of dollars.
section: The defense, and what it costs
text:
The defense, and what it costs
Svensson and Woodford showed two decades ago that when economic measurements are especially noisy or uncertain, the optimal policy is to pay them less attention. In the language of the Kalman filter, the central bank should put a smaller weight on the raw signal and a larger weight on its own model-based prior. The same idea applies, exactly, to the data-poisoning case. Filter harder, attack hurts less.
But filtering harder also means the Fed is less responsive to genuine shocks. A central bank that ignores its nowcast under attack also ignores it during a real productivity shift, a real demand shock, a real disinflation. The defense has a cost, and the size of the cost depends on what you think the probability of attack actually is.

title: If you can fool the Fed’s nowcast, you can move tens of billions of dollars.
text:
Three policy pillars
A defended Fed is the model’s prescription. It is also the easiest reform to implement, because it requires nothing of anyone outside the FOMC. The harder reforms work upstream of the Fed, on the integrity of the data itself. The original memo proposed three.
Cryptographic feed signatures. Every JSON or CSV nowcast feed the Fed ingests should originate from a hardware security module. The HSM holds the signing key in tamper-resistant hardware; NIST treats it as the gold standard for data integrity. The European Central Bank already requires this for its statistical data exchange. The cost is real: a 2023 market survey put the average HSM at thirteen thousand dollars per unit. The benefit is a tamper-evident audit trail that makes silent poisoning attacks much harder to execute.
Uncertainty-adaptive Taylor coefficients. Make the model’s prescription a rule. When the dispersion across nowcast inputs widens, the Fed should automatically down-weight noisy indicators in its policy response. This is exactly the Svensson-Woodford framework operationalized. The risk is recursion: if the dispersion measures themselves can be manipulated, the defense becomes the attack surface.
Public provenance ledgers. Publish the full ingestion log: every input, its source, its timestamp, its weight. The Russian Pravda operation was uncovered by the American Sunlight Project, an outside group with no special access. A public ledger lets external auditors do the same job for the Fed. Shayne Longpre and co-authors have argued for a multi-stakeholder data provenance standard “akin to the W3 consortium.” The risk is the inverse of the previous one: full transparency tells adversaries which inputs carry the most policy weight, and lets them target accordingly.
No single pillar is sufficient. Together they form the layered defense that the model says is worth paying for.

GitHub Pages does not work on private repos under a free GitHub plan. The push to gh-pages succeeded but enabling Pages returns HTTP 422 (“Your current plan does not support GitHub Pages for this repository”).
Three options to get a live URL:


If there is no sensitive content (and there is not — this is a research project), this is the fastest path.
gh repo edit jblakeslee89/poison-dsge --visibility public --accept-visibility-change-consequences
gh api -X POST /repos/jblakeslee89/poison-dsge/pages -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/'
Site is live in ~1 minute at https://jblakeslee89.github.io/poison-dsge/.

The dash app’s tour text and the project memory file describe the cumulative undershoot under realistic frictions as “~5× the toy memo’s cumulative distortion.” The current results/dash_cache_*.csv does not support this. Across cumulative windows of 4, 8, 12, and 16 quarters, the realistic-to-toy ratio is consistently 1.4× to 1.7×.
The story site uses the verifiable number (“74 bp / about 1.7×”). Before showing this to Wenger, decide whether:

Re-run the precompute with a different parameterization that produces 5× (if there was a calibration drift between the original memo and the current cache);
Update the dash app’s tour text and the memo to match the current 1.7× finding;
Reframe the headline finding around a different ratio that is 5× (e.g., welfare-cost ratio under a specific filter regime, peak deviation, variance ratio).

The 1.7× cumulative finding is still a meaningful and publishable result. The frame “the attack is worse, not better; it is just displaced in time” survives.

Try it yourself
text:
The interactive companion below lets you move three sliders across the model’s parameter space and watch how the attack response changes. The defaults are set to the empirical (Smets-Wouters posterior) calibration.
The full interactive demo is hosted separately as a Plotly Dash app. While that app is being deployed, here are static versions of the key configurations:

title: Try it yourself
text:
The three canonical scenarios

Memo (toy model, 2025)


        
        
        


                            
                                            


The original Spring 2025 calibration. Flat Phillips curve, no consumption habit, naive Fed. Produces the headline sign-flip on impact.


Realistic (Smets-Wouters posterior)


                            
                                            


Empirical Phillips slope, Smets-Wouters consumption habit, naive Fed. Impact sign-flip attenuates; the cumulative two-year response is the real story.


Defended (heavy filter)


                            
                                            


Realistic calibration with the Fed ignoring the raw nowcast signal entirely. The attack response collapses.

title: Try it yourself
text:
The defense-cost tradeoff


                            
                                            


Welfare loss with vs without attack at the realistic-with-light-filter calibration (\(\kappa = 0.15\), \(h = 0.7\), \(K = 0.1\)). At \(K = 0\), the red bar collapses to the blue. But there is a cost: the Fed becomes less responsive to genuine real shocks.
The full Dash app (deployed at HuggingFace Spaces when the deployment finalizes) lets you sweep all three sliders and read off the welfare crossover probability live.
